title: Notification System
prompt: Build the service every other team calls when they want to tell a user something, by push, SMS or email. It has to respect user preferences, never spam, and not lose the important ones.

clarify.q: What kinds of notifications: transactional (password reset, order shipped) or marketing campaigns too?
clarify.why: Transactional messages need seconds of latency and must not be lost. Campaigns are huge bursts that can wait. Mixing them on one queue lets a campaign delay a login code, so the answer decides whether you need separate lanes.

clarify.q: Which channels: mobile push, SMS, email, in-app? Do we own any of them or use providers?
clarify.why: We will almost certainly call APNs, FCM, an SMS gateway and an email provider. Their rate limits, failures and costs shape the worker design more than our own code does.

clarify.q: Is the caller sending a finished message, or an event plus a template we render?
clarify.why: Templates mean we own localisation and rendering. Finished text means callers can bypass branding and preferences. Most teams want templates owned centrally.

clarify.q: What delivery guarantee do callers expect: at most once or at least once?
clarify.why: At least once is the honest answer with external providers. That forces idempotency keys and a dedupe store, otherwise a retry sends the same SMS twice.

clarify.q: Do users control preferences per category and channel, plus quiet hours?
clarify.why: Preferences are checked on every send, so they must be cheap to read. Quiet hours add delayed scheduling by the user's time zone.

clarify.q: Do we need a history the user or support staff can see, and how long?
clarify.why: An in-app inbox or support lookup makes the notification log a product feature with read patterns, not just an audit trail.

clarify.q: Any per-user frequency caps, for example at most 3 marketing pushes a day?
clarify.why: Caps need a counter per user per category that every worker checks, which is a rate limiter keyed by user rather than by caller.

functional: Internal services send a notification by user id, category and template with variables; the service picks channels.
User preferences (opt-out per category and channel, quiet hours, time zone) are honoured on every send.
Each logical notification is delivered at most once per channel from the user's point of view, even when callers or workers retry.
Failed sends are retried with backoff and, for critical categories, fail over to another channel or provider.
Delivery status (queued, sent, delivered, failed, suppressed) can be queried per notification.
Bulk campaigns to millions of users can be scheduled without hurting transactional traffic.
nonFunctional: Transactional (OTP, security alerts): p99 under 5 s from API call to provider hand-off.
Marketing: may take up to 30 minutes to drain a 20 M user campaign.
No accepted request is lost: durable once the API returns 202.
API availability 99.95%; a single provider outage must not block other channels.
Duplicate rate below 1 in 100 000 sends per channel.
outOfScope: Building our own SMS or email delivery infrastructure (we use providers).
The campaign authoring UI and audience segmentation logic.
Rich in-app inbox UI beyond storing the log.

assumptions: 200 M notifications per day across all channels
Largest campaign: 20 M users in a 10 minute window
Stored notification record about 1 KB; keep 30 days
SMS costs roughly $0.01 per message on average

steps.label: SMS volume and cost
steps.result: SMS is the cost centre: ~$3 M a month

steps.label: Notification log
steps.result: ≈ 6 TB hot log: a wide-column store, not one Postgres box

steps.label: Dedupe keys
steps.math: 200 M × ~100 B (key + TTL overhead) = 20 GB/day; keep 48 h = 40 GB
steps.result: ≈ 40 GB: fits a small Redis cluster

estimates.takeaway: Average load is small (2.3 k/s). The design is driven by the burst (33 k/s campaigns) and by money (SMS at $100 k/day). So: queues absorb bursts, transactional and bulk traffic get separate queues and workers, and SMS sits behind strict caps and dedupe because every duplicate costs real cash.

api.body: { userId, category, template, vars, channels?, priority, sendAt? }
api.note: Idempotency-Key header is required. Same key within 48 h returns the original id and sends nothing new.
Expands to per-user sends in the background at the given throttle.
For support tools and caller debugging.

api.body: { categories: { marketing: { push: false } }, quietHours, timezone }
api.note: Called from the app settings screen.
Webhook from SMS/email providers; verified by HMAC signature, mapped back by provider message id.

entities.name: Notification
entities.store: Cassandra, partition by userId, cluster by createdAt desc
entities.why: Write-heavy, read mostly per user newest first. TTL removes old rows without a cleanup job.

entities.name: Preference
entities.why: Small, read on every send, rarely written. Cache hit rate is very high.

entities.name: DeviceToken
entities.why: One user has several devices; tokens die when apps are uninstalled and must be cleaned on provider errors.

entities.name: DedupeKey
entities.store: Redis, SET NX with 48 h TTL
entities.why: Workers claim a send before calling a provider so a redelivered queue message does not resend.

data.note: The notification log is append-heavy and read by user, so a wide-column store partitioned by userId fits. Preferences and device tokens are relational and tiny. The dedupe set lives in Redis because it is checked on the hot path and only needs to survive about two days.

hld.summary:
The Notification API validates the request, checks the caller's idempotency key, writes the notification row and an outbox row in one transaction, and returns 202. An outbox relay publishes to Kafka, split into a transactional topic and a bulk topic so campaigns never queue in front of an OTP.

A router consumes those topics, loads preferences, drops or delays what the user opted out of or what falls in quiet hours, renders the template, applies per-user frequency caps, and emits one message per channel onto channel topics. Channel workers (push, SMS, email) claim a dedupe key, call the provider with a per-provider rate limit, record the result, and retry with backoff through delay queues. Provider webhooks update final delivery status.

diagram.title: Send pipeline
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  S[Calling service] --> API[Notification API]
  API --> DB[("Notification log + outbox")]
  DB --> RL[Outbox relay]
  RL --> Q1[["Kafka: transactional"]]
  RL --> Q2[["Kafka: bulk"]]
  Q1 --> R[Router]
  Q2 --> R
  R --> P[("Preferences cache")]
  R --> CQ[["Channel topics"]]
  CQ --> W[Channel workers]
  W --> D[("Dedupe Redis")]
  W --> PR["Providers (APNs, FCM, SMS, email)"]
  PR --> CB[Callback handler]
  CB --> DB

flows.title: Sending a one-time login code
steps: Auth service calls POST /v1/notifications with category otp, priority high and an Idempotency-Key.
API writes the row and outbox entry in one transaction and returns 202 in ~20 ms.
Relay publishes to the transactional topic; the router sees OTP ignores quiet hours and picks SMS.
SMS worker does SET NX on notificationId:sms, calls the SMS provider, stores the provider message id.
Provider webhook later marks it delivered; if no receipt in 60 s and the user has the app, a push fallback is sent.

flows.title: Running a 20 M user campaign
steps: Marketing creates a campaign with throttlePerSec 30 000.
A campaign expander pages through the segment and writes per-user sends to the bulk topic at that rate.
The router drops users who opted out or are over their daily marketing cap, and delays users in quiet hours.
Push workers scale out on bulk-topic lag; transactional workers are a separate pool and are untouched.

flows.title: A worker crashes mid-send
steps: Worker claimed the dedupe key and called the provider, then died before committing its Kafka offset.
The message is redelivered to another worker, which finds the key already claimed.
If the key says sent, it acknowledges and moves on; if only claimed and older than 5 minutes, it checks the provider status by our reference id before deciding to resend.

deepDives.title: Not losing notifications and not sending them twice
deepDives.problem: Three places can lose or duplicate a message: between the caller and us, between our database and the queue, and between the worker and the provider. Providers do not join our transactions, so exactly-once is impossible end to end. We can only get at-least-once delivery with idempotent steps.

options.name: Write to DB, then publish to the queue in the API
options.how: API inserts the row, then calls Kafka produce, then returns.
cons: Crash between insert and publish leaves a row nobody sends
Publish succeeded but insert failed sends a message with no record

options.name: Transactional outbox + idempotent consumers
options.how: API writes the notification and an outbox row in the same DB transaction. A relay reads the outbox and publishes. Every consumer step is keyed by notificationId:channel.
pros: Retries anywhere are safe because each step checks its key
cons: One more moving part (the relay) to monitor
A few hundred ms extra latency on the happy path

options.name: Publish to Kafka only, no DB write in the request
options.how: API produces to Kafka with acks=all and returns; a consumer writes the log.
pros: Lowest latency, Kafka is the durable store
cons: Caller idempotency must be checked against a separate store anyway
Status lookups lag behind the queue

deepDives.choice: Use the outbox. At 2.3 k/s average the extra write is cheap and it gives a clean guarantee: if we said 202, it will be sent. Dedupe happens at three levels: caller Idempotency-Key in the API, notificationId:channel claim in the worker, and the provider's own idempotency field where it exists (many email APIs accept one). If peak traffic grew past what the database can absorb, I would switch to Kafka-first with a compacted idempotency topic.

deepDives.title: Keeping campaigns from starving transactional traffic
deepDives.problem: A campaign enqueues 20 M messages in ten minutes. If OTPs share that queue, a login code waits behind millions of promos. Providers also have account-level rate limits, so a campaign can use up the SMS quota an OTP needs.

options.name: One queue with a priority field
options.how: Workers sort or pick high-priority first inside one topic.
cons: Kafka partitions are FIFO, so priority inside a topic does not really work
Backlog still blocks

options.name: Separate topics and worker pools per priority
options.how: Transactional and bulk topics, each with its own consumer group and autoscaling; separate provider credentials or reserved quota for transactional.
pros: Hard isolation: a campaign can only slow itself
Each pool scales on its own lag
cons: Two pools to size and pay for
Need a rule for what counts as transactional, or teams mark everything high

options.name: Token-bucket shaping at the campaign expander
options.how: Campaigns are released at a throttle so the bulk lane never exceeds a share of provider capacity.
pros: Protects provider quotas and our own downstream
cons: Campaigns take longer to finish

deepDives.choice: Do both separate lanes and shaping. The transactional lane gets its own topic, workers and a reserved slice of each provider quota (for example 20% of SMS throughput). Campaigns go through a token bucket at the expander. Priority is decided by category, owned by us, not by a caller flag. If only one team ever sent campaigns and volumes were small, a single lane with a throttle would be enough.

deepDives.title: Preferences, quiet hours and frequency caps
deepDives.problem: Every send needs a preference check, a quiet-hours check in the user's time zone, and a per-user cap. That is 2.3 k to 33 k lookups per second. A wrong answer either spams someone who opted out (legal risk for email and SMS) or drops a message that mattered.

options.name: Check preferences in the API before accepting
options.how: API rejects or drops at request time.
pros: Saves queue work for dropped sends
cons: Preferences may change before a scheduled send fires
Callers see policy decisions they should not depend on

options.name: Check in the router right before fan-out to channels
options.how: Router reads preferences from a Redis cache backed by Postgres, computes local time, and checks a per-user counter.
cons: Router depends on the cache being up
Delayed sends need a scheduler

deepDives.choice: Decide in the router, as late as possible. Caps are Redis counters keyed cap:{userId}:{category}:{yyyymmdd} with INCR and a TTL. Quiet hours push the message onto a delay queue with a fire time computed from the user's IANA time zone. Security categories (OTP, password reset) skip quiet hours and caps by policy. If the preferences cache is down, transactional sends proceed with the last cached copy, while marketing sends pause, because sending a promo to someone who opted out is worse than sending it late.

deepDives.title: Retries, backoff and provider failover
deepDives.problem: Providers fail in different ways: 429 rate limits, 5xx outages, permanent errors like an invalid token or a bad phone number. Retrying permanent errors wastes money; not retrying transient ones loses messages.

options.name: Retry inline in the worker with sleep
options.how: Worker loops with exponential backoff before acking.
cons: Blocks a partition while sleeping
A provider outage stalls the whole lane

options.name: Retry topics with increasing delays plus a dead-letter queue
options.how: On transient failure, publish to retry-1m, retry-10m, retry-1h; after the last, to a DLQ. Classify errors first.
pros: Clear visibility of what is stuck
cons: Ordering per user is not preserved (fine for notifications)
More topics

options.name: Circuit breaker with failover provider
options.how: Track error rate per provider; when open, route that channel to a second provider.
cons: Two contracts and two integrations
Different delivery quality and receipts

deepDives.choice: Classify every error: permanent (invalid token: delete the token; invalid number: mark it) goes straight to failed; throttled slows the worker's token bucket; transient goes to delay topics with jittered exponential backoff, max about 6 attempts over 2 hours. Add a circuit breaker and a second SMS provider because SMS carries OTPs. For push there is no second provider for APNs, so we just retry. If OTP delivery were less critical, one SMS provider would save the integration work.

failures: SMS provider has a regional outage
Circuit breaker opens on error rate, transactional SMS fails over to the second provider, bulk SMS pauses and backs up in Kafka.
Redis dedupe cluster loses data in a failover
Workers fall back to checking the notification log's channel status before sending; accept a small duplicate window; alert.
A bad campaign template renders blank or broken text
Render a preview sample before release, canary the first 0.1% of the campaign, and provide a kill switch per campaign id.
A team bug calls the API in a loop for the same user
Per-caller rate limits at the API plus per-user caps in the router; idempotency keys make identical retries free.
Push tokens go stale after uninstalls
Delete tokens on APNs/FCM 'unregistered' responses and prune tokens not seen in 60 days.
Kafka consumer lag grows on the bulk lane
Autoscale workers on lag; it is acceptable for bulk to fall behind as long as the transactional lane has its own pool.
scale: 10× (2 B/day, 330 k/s campaign peaks): partition topics further, shard the dedupe Redis by key hash, and negotiate higher provider quotas; SMS cost becomes a business conversation before a technical one.
Multi-region: run the pipeline in each region with users homed to one region so preferences and caps stay local; replicate the notification log asynchronously.
Many more channels (WhatsApp, Slack, webhooks): keep channel workers as plugins behind one interface: render, send, classify error, parse receipt.

followups.q: How do you guarantee an OTP arrives within seconds?
answer: Separate transactional lane with reserved provider quota.
Skip quiet hours and caps for that category.
Watch time-to-provider p99 as an SLO and fail over to a second SMS provider or push if receipts do not arrive.

followups.q: How do you avoid sending the same push to a user with three devices three times?
answer: It is one notification per device by design; that is expected.
But dedupe is per notificationId plus channel plus device token, so a retry never resends to the same device.
For in-app the client marks the notification read across devices via the log.

followups.q: How do you handle time zones for 'send at 9 am local time'?
answer: The campaign expander buckets users by zone and releases each bucket when it hits 9 am there.
Users with unknown zones get a default per country.

followups.q: How would you measure delivery success?
answer: Track funnel per channel: accepted, routed, suppressed, sent to provider, delivered, opened.
Delivery comes from provider webhooks; opens from tracking pixels or app events.
Alert on drops between stages, not just on errors.

followups.q: What about legal requirements for marketing email and SMS?
answer: Unsubscribe links and STOP keywords must update preferences immediately.
Keep proof of consent with a timestamp.
Marketing pauses rather than guesses when preferences are unavailable.

mistakes: Claiming exactly-once delivery to a third-party provider instead of at-least-once with idempotency.
Putting OTPs and marketing on the same queue, so a campaign delays login codes.
Retrying every error, including invalid phone numbers and dead device tokens, which burns money.
Checking preferences only at request time, then sending a scheduled message after the user opted out.
Sizing for the 2.3 k/s average and ignoring the 33 k/s campaign burst.

mid: Asked whether marketing and transactional traffic share the system
Put a durable queue between the API and the channel senders
Stored user preferences and checked them before sending
Retried failed sends with exponential backoff and a dead-letter queue
Computed average and peak send rates with the arithmetic shown
senior: Used an outbox (or equivalent) so accepted requests are never lost
Made every step idempotent with a key per notification and channel
Separated transactional and bulk lanes with their own workers and provider quota
Classified provider errors into permanent, throttled and transient with different handling
Explained quiet hours and frequency caps with a concrete storage key and TTL
staff: Brought up SMS cost and used it to justify caps and dedupe strictness
Defined SLOs per category (OTP p99 vs campaign drain time) and an end-to-end delivery funnel
Planned provider failover with circuit breakers and said where it is not possible (APNs)
Stated the fail-open versus fail-closed policy per category when the preference store is down
